description: 150 famous brand slogans and taglines from Nike, Apple, BMW, GEICO and more, grouped by industry, plus the 5-step process I use to write a slogan.
body:
A good slogan can outlive the campaign it was written for by decades.

Below are 150 famous brand slogans and taglines grouped by industry, followed by the difference between a slogan and a tagline and the process I use to write one.

What Makes a Slogan Effective?

Before diving into our list, let's understand what makes a slogan truly memorable. The best brand slogans share these qualities:

Brevity: Most iconic slogans are just 3-5 words
Emotional resonance: They connect with feelings, not just features
Memorability: Easy to recall and repeat
Timelessness: They remain relevant across decades
Brand alignment: They perfectly capture the brand's essence

I write the slogan last, once purpose, positioning and personality are defined, which is why it closes my guide on how to develop a brand strategy.

Slogan vs. Tagline: What's the Difference?

People use the two words interchangeably, and this list mixes both.

A tagline is the long-lived line that sits next to the logo and sums up the whole brand, like Nike's "Just Do It".

A slogan usually belongs to one campaign or product and changes when the campaign does, like Coca-Cola moving from "Open Happiness" to "Taste the Feeling".

Neither is the same as a mission statement or a vision statement, which explain why a company exists rather than how it sounds to customers.

How to Write a Slogan for Your Brand

The lines above look effortless, but each one compresses a strategic decision into a few words.

This is the process I use with clients.

1. Start From Your Positioning

A slogan should claim the one thing you want to own, so write your positioning statement first.

BMW's "The Ultimate Driving Machine" works because BMW chose performance over comfort or status.

2. Pick One Idea, Not Three

The strongest slogans on this list carry a single promise: relief, speed, belonging or courage.

If you need a comma to fit everything in, you probably have more than one idea.

3. Write in Your Brand Voice

"Finger Lickin' Good" and "The Best or Nothing" are both quality claims, yet nobody would confuse KFC with Mercedes-Benz.

Define your brand voice and brand personality before drafting, so the line sounds like you.

4. Use Sound to Make It Stick

Rhyme ("Grace, Space, Pace"), repetition ("It Keeps Going and Going and Going") and questions ("Got Milk?") make a line easier to remember and repeat.

5. Test It Out Loud

Write 30 to 50 options, shortlist five, and say each one out loud next to your name and logo.

Check the shortlist for conflicts before you commit; my guide on how to trademark a logo covers the basics.

That is why the tagline is the last exercise in my brand strategy framework, not the first.

Conclusion

These 150 slogans span tech, food, cars, finance, travel and public campaigns, but the best of them share the same traits: one idea, said in the brand's own voice, short enough to repeat.

Use them as reference, not templates: a slogan only works when it grows out of a clear positioning.

If you want help defining that positioning and the line that comes from it, start with my brand strategy guide.
